units.excerpt: As AI models become more capable, Anthropic believes that they will create major economic and social value, but will also present increasingly severe risks.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic believes more capable AI models will bring major benefits but also increasingly severe risks.

units.excerpt: With this document we are making a public commitment to a concrete framework for managing these risks—one that will evolve over time, but that seeks to establish clear expectations and accountability in its initial form.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic is publicly committing to an evolving framework meant to establish clear initial expectations and accountability.

units.excerpt: We focus these commitments specifically on catastrophic risks1, defined as large-scale devastation (for example, thousands of deaths or hundreds of billions of dollars in damage) that is directly caused by an AI model and wouldn’t have occurred without it.
units.paraphrase: The commitments are focused specifically on catastrophic risks, defined as large-scale devastation directly and necessarily caused by an AI model.

units.excerpt: AI represents a spectrum of risks and these commitments are designed to deal with the more extreme end of this spectrum.
units.paraphrase: The document addresses the most extreme portion of the AI risk spectrum.

units.excerpt: This work is complementary to our work on other areas of AI safety, including mitigating harms like misinformation, bias, and toxicity, studying societal impacts, protecting customer privacy, building robust and reliable systems, and developing techniques like Constitutional AI for alignment with human values.
units.paraphrase: This document complements other Anthropic safety work such as bias mitigation, privacy protection, robustness, and Constitutional AI alignment work.

units.excerpt: Note that these commitments primarily relate to internal testing and development practices for future more powerful versions of Claude.
units.paraphrase: The commitments mainly govern internal testing and development of future, more capable Claude versions.

units.excerpt: They do not alter current uses of Claude or any of Anthropic’s present offerings (beyond safety practices we already engage in).
units.paraphrase: The policy does not change existing Claude usage or Anthropic's current offerings beyond already-existing safety practices.

units.excerpt: Our commitments are designed in the spirit of the Responsible Scaling Policy (RSP) framework being developed by Paul Christiano and ARC Evals, as well as emerging government policy proposals on responsible AI development in the UK, EU, and US.
units.paraphrase: The commitments draw on the RSP framework being developed by Paul Christiano and ARC Evals, and on emerging UK, EU, and US policy proposals.

units.excerpt: We thank ARC Evals for substantial advice and collaboration on the development of our commitments.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic thanks ARC Evals for its advice and collaboration.

units.excerpt: We have in mind events of the magnitude of thousands of deaths or hundreds of billions of dollars in damage, as described in the main text, but the long tail of catastrophes could be significantly worse than even this.
units.paraphrase: The footnote clarifies that the stated magnitude is illustrative and worse catastrophes are possible.

units.excerpt: We also have in mind direct damage rather than broader societal processes where AI may play an indirect role (the latter is also important, but outside the scope of this document).
units.paraphrase: The footnote excludes indirect societal harms from AI from the scope of the catastrophic risk definition.

units.excerpt: We use the terms “catastrophe” and “catastrophic harm”, throughout the text to refer to events of this magnitude, and “risk of catastrophe” and “catastrophic risk” to refer to risk of these events.
units.paraphrase: The footnote defines the terminology used for catastrophe-related terms throughout the document.

units.excerpt: Central to our plan is the concept of AI safety levels (ASL), which are modeled loosely after the US government’s biosafety level (BSL) standards for handling of dangerous biological materials.
units.paraphrase: The framework centers on AI safety levels (ASL), modeled loosely on US biosafety level standards.

units.excerpt: We define a series of AI capability thresholds that represent increasing potential risks, such that each ASL requires more stringent safety, security, and operational measures than the previous one.
units.paraphrase: Each successive ASL threshold requires progressively stricter safety, security, and operational measures.

units.excerpt: Of course, higher ASL models are also likely to be associated with increasingly powerful beneficial applications (including potentially the ability to prevent catastrophic risks), so our goal is not to prohibit development of these models, but rather to safely enable their use with appropriate precautions.
units.paraphrase: The goal is not to prohibit higher-ASL model development but to safely enable it with appropriate precautions, given the beneficial applications involved.

units.context_stem: For each ASL, the framework considers two broad classes of risks:
units.excerpt: Deployment risks: Risks that arise from active use of powerful AI models. This includes harm caused by users querying an API or other public interface, as well as misuse by internal users (compromised or malicious).
units.paraphrase: Deployment risks arise from active use of powerful models, including harm from API queries or misuse by internal users.

units.context_stem: For each ASL, the framework considers two broad classes of risks: Deployment risks
units.excerpt: Our deployment safety measures are designed to address these risks by governing when we can safely deploy a powerful AI model.
units.paraphrase: Deployment safety measures govern when a powerful model can be safely deployed.

units.context_stem: For each ASL, the framework considers two broad classes of risks:
units.excerpt: Containment risks: Risks that arise from merely possessing a powerful AI model. Examples include (1) building an AI model that, due to its general capabilities, could enable the production of weapons of mass destruction if stolen and used by a malicious actor, or (2) building a model which autonomously escapes during internal use.
units.paraphrase: Containment risks arise merely from possessing a powerful model, such as enabling WMD production if stolen or a model autonomously escaping during internal use.

units.context_stem: For each ASL, the framework considers two broad classes of risks: Containment risks
units.excerpt: Our containment measures are designed to address these risks by governing when we can safely train or continue training a model.
units.paraphrase: Containment measures govern when it is safe to train or continue training a model.

units.excerpt: Complying with higher ASLs is not just a procedural matter, but may sometimes require research or technical breakthroughs to give affirmative evidence of a model’s safety (which is generally not possible today), demonstrated inability to elicit catastrophic risks during red-teaming (as opposed to merely a commitment to perform red-teaming), and/or unusually stringent information security controls.
units.paraphrase: Meeting higher ASL requirements may require research breakthroughs, demonstrated red-teaming safety, or very strict security controls, not just procedural compliance.

units.excerpt: Anthropic’s commitment to follow the ASL scheme thus implies that we commit to pause the scaling2 and/or delay the deployment of new models whenever our scaling ability outstrips our ability to comply with the safety procedures for the corresponding ASL.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic commits to pausing scaling and/or delaying deployment whenever its capability growth exceeds its ability to meet the corresponding ASL's safety procedures.

units.excerpt: We use "scaling" to refer to broadly increasing the capabilities and intelligence of AI systems, either through increasing compute used in training or through algorithmic improvements.
units.paraphrase: The footnote defines "scaling" as increasing AI capabilities via compute or algorithmic improvements.

units.excerpt: One challenge with the ASL scheme as compared to BSL is that ASLs above our current capabilities represent systems that have never been built before – in contrast to BSL, where the highest levels include specific dangerous pathogens that exist today.
units.paraphrase: Unlike BSL, higher ASL levels describe systems that do not yet exist, unlike known dangerous pathogens in BSL.

units.excerpt: The ASL system thus has an unavoidable component of “building the airplane while flying it”— we will have to start acting on many provisions of this policy before others can reasonably be specified.
units.paraphrase: The ASL system inherently requires acting on some provisions before others can be fully specified.

units.excerpt: Rather than try to define all future ASLs and their safety measures now (which would almost certainly not stand the test of time), we will instead take an approach of iterative commitments.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will use iterative commitments rather than defining all future ASLs upfront.

units.excerpt: By iterative, we mean we will define ASL-2 (current system) and ASL-3 (next level of risk) now, and commit to define ASL-4 by the time we reach ASL-3, and so on.
units.paraphrase: Iterative means ASL-2 and ASL-3 are defined now, with ASL-4 to be defined by the time ASL-3 is reached, and so forth.

units.excerpt: Towards the end of this document we speculate about ASL-4+, but only to give a flavor of our current thinking and early preparation (which will likely change a lot as we get closer to ASL-4).
units.paraphrase: Later sections speculate about ASL-4 and beyond only to illustrate current thinking, which is expected to change substantially.

units.excerpt: This document will be periodically updated as we learn more, according to an “Update Process” described below.
units.paraphrase: The document will be periodically updated per a described Update Process.

units.excerpt: Updates will involve both defining higher ASL levels, and making course corrections to existing levels and safety measures as we learn more.
units.paraphrase: Updates will define higher ASL levels and revise existing levels and measures.

units.excerpt: We also welcome input on this document from other groups working on AI risk assessment and safety/security measures.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic welcomes input from other groups working on AI risk assessment and safety measures.

units.excerpt: Our current understanding suggests at least two general sources of catastrophic risk from increasingly powerful AI models.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic identifies at least two general sources of catastrophic risk from increasingly powerful models.

units.excerpt: For our initial commitments, we design our evaluations and safety measures with these risks in mind:
units.paraphrase: Initial commitments' evaluations and safety measures are designed around these two risk sources.

units.context_stem: Our current understanding suggests at least two general sources of catastrophic risk:
units.excerpt: Misuse: AI systems are dual-use technologies, and so as they become more powerful, there is an increasing risk that they will be used to intentionally cause large-scale harm, for example by helping individuals create CBRN3 or cyber threats.
units.paraphrase: Misuse risk arises because dual-use AI systems could increasingly help people cause large-scale harm, such as CBRN or cyber threats.

units.context_stem: Our current understanding suggests at least two general sources of catastrophic risk:
units.excerpt: Autonomy and replication: As AI systems continue to scale, they may become capable of increased autonomy that enables them to proliferate and, due to imperfections in current methods for steering such systems, potentially behave in ways contrary to the intent of their designers or users.
units.paraphrase: Autonomy and replication risk arises as scaling AI systems may enable increased autonomy and proliferation, with potential to act against designer or user intent due to imperfect steering methods.

units.excerpt: Such systems could become a source of catastrophic risk even if no one deliberately intends to misuse them.
units.paraphrase: Autonomy-related risk could produce catastrophe even absent any deliberate misuse.

units.excerpt: We are likely to revise and refine these ideas as our understanding of AI systems develops.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic expects to revise these risk categorizations as understanding improves.

units.excerpt: Our initial responsible scaling commitments consist of the following elements, which are visualized below and expanded on in the rest of this document.
units.paraphrase: The initial commitments consist of several elements, visualized and explained further in the document.

units.context_stem: Our initial responsible scaling commitments consist of the following elements:
units.excerpt: ASL-2: The security and safety measures we commit to take with current state-of-the-art models, many of which we have previously committed to.
units.paraphrase: ASL-2 comprises security and safety measures for current state-of-the-art models, several of which were previously committed to.

units.context_stem: Our initial responsible scaling commitments consist of the following elements:
units.excerpt: ASL-3: A set of dangerous capabilities we think could arise in near-future models, along with the Containment Measures we commit to implement before training such a model, and the Deployment Measures we commit to take before deploying it.
units.paraphrase: ASL-3 defines dangerous capabilities anticipated in near-future models plus the containment measures required before training and deployment measures required before deploying such models.

units.excerpt: CBRN refers to the chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear domains. We use it mostly to refer to threats in those domains.
units.paraphrase: The footnote defines CBRN as chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear domains.

units.excerpt: We acknowledge that some of these domains will become more or less relevant for evaluation over time.
units.paraphrase: The footnote notes that CBRN domain relevance for evaluation may shift over time.

units.context_stem: Our initial responsible scaling commitments consist of the following elements:
units.excerpt: ASL-4 iterative commitment: We commit to define ASL-4 evaluations before we first train ASL-3 models (i.e. before continuing training beyond when ASL-3 evaluations are triggered).
units.paraphrase: Anthropic commits to defining ASL-4 evaluations before beginning training of ASL-3 models.

units.context_stem: Our initial responsible scaling commitments consist of the following elements: ASL-4 iterative commitment
units.excerpt: Similarly, we commit to define ASL-5 evaluations before training ASL-4 models, and so forth.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will similarly define ASL-5 evaluations before training ASL-4 models, continuing this pattern.

units.context_stem: Our initial responsible scaling commitments consist of the following elements:
units.excerpt: Evaluation protocol: A protocol for when and how to evaluate models for dangerous capabilities, ensuring we detect warning signs before models require higher ASL safety measures.
units.paraphrase: An evaluation protocol specifies when and how to test models for dangerous capabilities to catch warning signs early.

units.context_stem: Our initial responsible scaling commitments consist of the following elements: Evaluation protocol
units.excerpt: We commit to pause training before a model's capability level outstrips the Containment Measures we have implemented.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic commits to pausing training before a model's capability exceeds implemented containment measures.

units.context_stem: Our initial responsible scaling commitments consist of the following elements:
units.excerpt: Procedural commitments: A set of transparency and procedural measures to ensure verifiable compliance with the commitments in the previous bullet points.
units.paraphrase: Procedural commitments are transparency and procedural measures ensuring verifiable compliance with the other commitments.

units.context_stem: Our initial responsible scaling commitments consist of the following elements: Procedural commitments
units.excerpt: Notably, we commit to a formal process for modifying the current safety levels in response to new information, and defining future levels.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic commits to a formal process for modifying current safety levels and defining future levels.

units.excerpt: The scheme above is designed to ensure that we will always have a set of safety guardrails that govern training and deployment of our next model, without having to define all ASLs at the outset.
units.paraphrase: The scheme ensures ongoing safety guardrails for the next model without requiring all ASLs to be predefined.

units.excerpt: Near the bottom of this document, we do provide a guess about higher ASLs, but we emphasize that these are so speculative that they are likely to bear little resemblance to the final version.
units.paraphrase: Speculation about higher ASLs later in the document is expected to differ substantially from the eventual final version.

units.excerpt: Our hope is that the broad ASL framework can scale to extremely powerful AI, even though the actual content of the higher ASLs will need to be developed over time.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic hopes the ASL framework itself can scale to very powerful AI even as higher-level content is developed later.

units.section_heading: Table: AI Safety Level Framework Overview
units.excerpt: Models which manifestly and obviously pose no risk of catastrophe. For example, an LLM from 2018, or an AI system trained only to play chess.
units.paraphrase: ASL-1 models manifestly pose no catastrophic risk, exemplified by a 2018 LLM or a chess-only AI.

units.section_heading: Table: AI Safety Level Framework Overview
units.context_stem: Row: ASL-1. Column: Containment Measures Required to store model weights.
units.excerpt: None
units.paraphrase: No containment measures are required at ASL-1.

units.section_heading: Table: AI Safety Level Framework Overview
units.context_stem: Row: ASL-1. Column: Deployment Measures Required for internal/external use.
units.excerpt: None
units.paraphrase: No deployment measures are required at ASL-1.

units.section_heading: Table: AI Safety Level Framework Overview
units.context_stem: Row: ASL-2 (Our current safety level). Column: Dangerous Capabilities.
units.excerpt: No capabilities likely to cause catastrophe, although early indications of these capabilities. For example, an AI system that can provide bioweapon-related information that couldn’t be found via a search engine, but does so too unreliably to be useful in practice.
units.paraphrase: ASL-2 models show early but not yet actionable signs of catastrophic capability, such as unreliable bioweapon-related information beyond search engine availability.

units.section_heading: Table: AI Safety Level Framework Overview
units.context_stem: Row: ASL-2 (We are currently preparing these measures). Column: Containment Measures Required to store model weights.
units.excerpt: Evaluate for ASL-3 warning signs when training, using methods and Evaluation Protocol described below.
units.paraphrase: During training, ASL-2 requires evaluating for ASL-3 warning signs using the described methods.

units.section_heading: Table: AI Safety Level Framework Overview
units.context_stem: Row: ASL-2. Column: Containment Measures Required to store model weights.
units.excerpt: Harden security against opportunistic attackers.
units.paraphrase: ASL-2 containment requires hardening security against opportunistic attackers.

units.section_heading: Table: AI Safety Level Framework Overview
units.context_stem: Row: ASL-2. Column: Deployment Measures Required for internal/external use.
units.excerpt: Follow current deployment best practices e.g. model cards, acceptable use policies, misuse escalation procedures, vulnerability reporting, harm refusal techniques, T&S tooling, and partner safety evaluation.
units.paraphrase: ASL-2 deployment requires following current best practices, including model cards, acceptable use policies, misuse escalation, vulnerability reporting, harm refusal techniques, T&S tooling, and partner safety evaluation.

units.section_heading: Table: AI Safety Level Framework Overview
units.context_stem: Row: ASL-2. Column: Deployment Measures Required for internal/external use.
units.excerpt: These overlap significantly with our White House voluntary commitments.
units.paraphrase: ASL-2 deployment measures largely overlap with the White House voluntary commitments.

units.section_heading: Table: AI Safety Level Framework Overview
units.context_stem: Row: ASL-3 (We are currently preparing these measures). Column: Dangerous Capabilities.
units.excerpt: Low-level autonomous capabilities or Access to the model would substantially increase the risk of catastrophic misuse, either by proliferating capabilities, lowering costs, or enabling new methods of attack, as compared to a non-LLM baseline of risk.
units.paraphrase: ASL-3 covers low-level autonomous capabilities or model access that substantially raises catastrophic misuse risk relative to a non-LLM baseline.

units.section_heading: Table: AI Safety Level Framework Overview
units.context_stem: Row: ASL-3. Column: Containment Measures Required to store model weights.
units.excerpt: Harden security such that non-state attackers are unlikely to be able to steal model weights and advanced threat actors (e.g. states) cannot steal them without significant expense.
units.paraphrase: ASL-3 containment requires security hardened so non-state attackers cannot easily steal weights and state actors face significant costs to do so.

units.section_heading: Table: AI Safety Level Framework Overview
units.context_stem: Row: ASL-3. Column: Containment Measures Required to store model weights.
units.excerpt: Evaluate for ASL-4 warning signs when training, likely similar to but much more involved than the methods described below.
units.paraphrase: ASL-3 containment requires evaluating for ASL-4 warning signs during training, using more involved methods than described for ASL-3.

units.section_heading: Table: AI Safety Level Framework Overview
units.context_stem: Row: ASL-3. Column: Containment Measures Required to store model weights.
units.excerpt: Implement internal compartmentalization for training techniques and model hyperparameters.
units.paraphrase: ASL-3 containment requires internal compartmentalization of training techniques and hyperparameters.

units.section_heading: Table: AI Safety Level Framework Overview
units.context_stem: Row: ASL-3. Column: Deployment Measures Required for internal/external use.
units.excerpt: Implement strong misuse prevention measures, including internal usage controls, automated detection, a vulnerability disclosure process, and maximum jailbreak response times.
units.paraphrase: ASL-3 deployment requires strong misuse prevention, including internal usage controls, automated detection, vulnerability disclosure, and maximum jailbreak response times.

units.section_heading: Table: AI Safety Level Framework Overview
units.context_stem: Row: ASL-3. Column: Deployment Measures Required for internal/external use.
units.excerpt: Each deployed modality (e.g. API, fine-tuning) must pass intensive expert red-teaming and evaluation measures for catastrophic risks.
units.paraphrase: Every deployed modality must pass intensive expert red-teaming and catastrophic-risk evaluation before ASL-3 deployment.

units.section_heading: Table: AI Safety Level Framework Overview
units.excerpt: Capabilities and warning sign evaluations defined before training ASL-3 models
units.paraphrase: ASL-4 capabilities and warning sign evaluations will be defined before training of ASL-3 models begins.

units.section_heading: Table: AI Safety Level Framework Overview
units.excerpt: A brief visualization of the AI Safety Levels framework. All safety measures are cumulative above the previous level.
units.paraphrase: The table visualizes the ASL framework, noting that safety measures accumulate across levels.

units.excerpt: As can be seen in the table, our most significant immediate commitments include a high standard of security for ASL-3 containment, and a commitment not to deploy ASL-3 models until thorough red-teaming finds no risk of catastrophe.
units.paraphrase: The most significant near-term commitments are strong ASL-3 security and not deploying ASL-3 models until red-teaming finds no catastrophic risk.

units.excerpt: We expect these to be difficult, binding constraints that may become relevant in the next year or two, requiring substantial effort, investment, and planning to meet.
units.paraphrase: These commitments are expected to be difficult, binding, and relevant within one to two years, requiring significant effort to satisfy.

units.locator: ASL-2 Capabilities and Threat Models / para 1
units.excerpt: We define ASL-24 as models that do not yet pose a risk of catastrophe, but do exhibit early signs of the necessary capabilities required for catastrophic harms.
units.paraphrase: ASL-2 models are defined as not yet posing catastrophic risk but showing early signs of the necessary capabilities for catastrophic harm.

units.locator: ASL-2 Capabilities and Threat Models / para 1
units.excerpt: For example, ASL-2 models may (in absence of safeguards) (a) provide information related to catastrophic misuse, but not in a way that significantly elevates risk compared to existing sources of knowledge such as search engines5, or (b) provide information about catastrophic misuse cases that cannot be easily found in another way, but is inconsistent or unreliable enough to not yet present a significantly elevated risk of actual harm.
units.paraphrase: ASL-2 models, absent safeguards, may provide catastrophic-misuse information no more risky than existing sources, or provide hard-to-find but unreliable information that does not yet significantly elevate risk.

units.locator: ASL-2 Capabilities and Threat Models / para 2
units.excerpt: Informed by our work on frontier red teaming, our current estimate is that Claude 2 and similar frontier models exhibit (a) and sometimes exhibit (b), but do not appear (yet) to present significant actual risks of catastrophe through misuse or autonomous self-replication.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic estimates Claude 2 and similar models show trait (a) and sometimes (b) but do not yet present significant catastrophic risk via misuse or self-replication.

units.locator: ASL-2 Capabilities and Threat Models / para 2
units.excerpt: Thus, we classify Claude 2 as ASL-2, and we believe the same is likely true of other frontier LLMs that exist today.
units.paraphrase: Claude 2 is classified as ASL-2, and other current frontier LLMs are believed likely to be similarly classified.

units.locator: ASL-2 Capabilities and Threat Models / para 2
units.excerpt: It is unclear how much scale-up would be required to present a significant risk of catastrophe, but these results suggest a real risk that the next generation of models could qualify.
units.paraphrase: It is uncertain how much further scaling would create significant catastrophic risk, but the next model generation could plausibly qualify.

units.locator: ASL-2 Capabilities and Threat Models / para 2
units.excerpt: For this reason, we commit to periodic evaluations of our future models for ASL-3 warning signs.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic commits to periodically evaluating future models for ASL-3 warning signs.

units.excerpt: We do not believe that merely possessing today’s models poses significant risk of catastrophe; however, in keeping with our commitments earlier this year, we will treat AI model weights as core intellectual property with regards to cybersecurity and insider threat risks.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic does not think possessing current models poses significant catastrophic risk, but will still treat model weights as core IP for cybersecurity and insider threat purposes, per earlier commitments.

units.excerpt: You can read more about our concrete security commitments in the appendix, which include limiting access to model weights to those whose job function requires it, establishing a robust insider threat detection program, and storing and working with the weights in an appropriately secure environment to reduce the risk of unsanctioned release.
units.paraphrase: The appendix details security commitments including need-based access limits, insider threat detection, and secure storage/handling of weights to reduce unsanctioned release risk.

units.excerpt: More broadly, we plan to use future ASLs in part to guide and focus our safety and security investments.
units.paraphrase: Future ASLs will help guide and focus safety and security investment decisions.

units.excerpt: Additionally, we commit to periodically evaluating for ASL-3 warning signs (described in the Evaluation Protocol below).
units.paraphrase: Anthropic commits to periodic evaluation for ASL-3 warning signs as described in the Evaluation Protocol.

units.excerpt: Note: We intend "ASL-N" to primarily refer to a specific set of safety measures that we might implement, similar to how BSL-N is a specification of safety measures required to meet a certain standard.
units.paraphrase: The footnote clarifies ASL-N primarily denotes a set of safety measures, analogous to BSL-N specifications.

units.excerpt: However, it is colloquially useful to refer to an AI model as ASL-N if it possesses capabilities meriting ASL-N safety measures.
units.paraphrase: It is also colloquially acceptable to call a model "ASL-N" if its capabilities merit ASL-N measures.

units.excerpt: For example, we might call a model an "ASL-3 model" if it has capabilities requiring ASL-3 safety measures and does not have capabilities meriting ASL-4 safety measures.
units.paraphrase: A model may be called "ASL-3" if it requires ASL-3 measures but not ASL-4 measures.

units.excerpt: Note that ASLs are defined by risk relative to baseline, excluding other advanced AI systems.
units.paraphrase: ASL definitions measure risk relative to a baseline that excludes other advanced AI systems.

units.excerpt: This means that a model that initially merits ASL-3 containment and deployment measures for national security reasons might later be reduced to ASL-2 if defenses against national security risks (such as biological or cyber defenses) advance, or if dangerous information becomes more widely available.
units.paraphrase: A model classified ASL-3 for national security reasons could later be reclassified ASL-2 if defenses improve or dangerous information becomes more widely available.

units.excerpt: However, to avoid a “race to the bottom”, the latter should not include the effects of other companies’ language models; just because other language models pose a catastrophic risk does not mean it is acceptable for ours to.
units.paraphrase: To avoid a race to the bottom, the availability of dangerous information from other companies' models does not justify accepting the same risk in Anthropic's own models.

units.excerpt: While ASL-2 models do not carry significant risk of causing a catastrophe, their deployment still poses a range of trust and safety, legal, and ethical risks.
units.paraphrase: ASL-2 models pose non-catastrophic but still real trust, safety, legal, and ethical deployment risks.

units.excerpt: To address these risks, our ASL-2 deployment commitments include:
units.paraphrase: The following list constitutes the ASL-2 deployment commitments addressing these risks.

units.excerpt: Model cards: Publish model cards for significant new models describing capabilities, limitations, evaluations, and intended use cases.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will publish model cards describing capabilities, limitations, evaluations, and intended uses for significant new models.

units.excerpt: The most recent model card for Claude 2 is available here.
units.paraphrase: The most recent Claude 2 model card is publicly available.

units.excerpt: Acceptable use: Maintain and enforce an acceptable use policy (AUP) that restricts, at a minimum, catastrophic and high harm use cases, including using the model to generate content that could cause severe risks to the continued existence of humankind, or direct and severe harm to individuals.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will maintain and enforce an acceptable use policy restricting at least catastrophic and high-harm uses, including existential and severe individual harm content.

units.excerpt: See our current AUP here which briefly describes our enforcement measures, which include maintaining the option to restrict access if extreme misuse issues emerge.
units.paraphrase: The AUP describes enforcement measures, including the option to restrict access if extreme misuse arises.

units.excerpt: Vulnerability reporting: Provide clearly indicated paths for our consumer and API products where users can report harmful or dangerous model outputs or use cases.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will provide clear reporting paths for harmful or dangerous outputs across consumer and API products.

units.excerpt: Users of claude.ai can report issues directly in the product, and API users can report issues to usersafety@anthropic.com.
units.paraphrase: Claude.ai users can report issues in-product, and API users can email usersafety@anthropic.com.

units.excerpt: Harm refusal techniques: Train models to refuse requests to aid in causing harm, such as with Constitutional AI or other improved techniques.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will train models to refuse harmful requests using Constitutional AI or similar techniques.

units.excerpt: T&S tooling: Require model enhanced trust and safety detection and enforcement. Claude.ai, our native API, and our distribution partners currently use a classifier model to identify harmful user prompts and model completions6.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic requires enhanced trust and safety detection tooling; Claude.ai, the API, and distribution partners currently use a classifier to detect harmful prompts and completions.

units.excerpt: If automated fine-tuning is provided, data should similarly be filtered for harmfulness, and models should be subject to automated evaluation to ensure harmlessness features are not degraded.
units.paraphrase: If automated fine-tuning is offered, training data must be filtered for harm and models must undergo automated evaluation to preserve harmlessness.

units.excerpt: Our ASL-2 deployment measures overlap substantially with the White House voluntary commitments that we and other companies made in July, which we also continue to maintain.
units.paraphrase: ASL-2 deployment measures largely overlap with the July White House voluntary commitments, which Anthropic continues to uphold.

units.excerpt: There are a very limited number of use cases where, at ASL-2, we would consider disabling this tooling.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic would consider disabling T&S tooling only in a very limited number of ASL-2 use cases.

units.excerpt: These may be negotiated on a case by case basis and must be considered exclusively for extremely low risk use cases that actively involve Anthropic personnel.
units.paraphrase: Exceptions to T&S tooling would be negotiated case-by-case and limited to extremely low-risk cases actively involving Anthropic personnel.

units.locator: ASL-3 Capabilities and Threat Models / para 1
units.excerpt: We define an ASL-3 model as one that can either immediately, or with additional post-training techniques corresponding to less than 1% of the total training cost, do at least one of the following two things.
units.paraphrase: An ASL-3 model is defined as one that, immediately or with post-training techniques costing less than 1% of total training cost, can do at least one of two specified things.

units.locator: ASL-3 Capabilities and Threat Models / para 1
units.excerpt: (By post-training techniques we mean the best capabilities elicitation techniques we are aware of at the time, including but not limited to fine-tuning, scaffolding, tool use, and prompt engineering.)
units.paraphrase: Post-training techniques refer to the best-known capability elicitation methods, such as fine-tuning, scaffolding, tool use, and prompt engineering.

units.locator: ASL-3 Capabilities and Threat Models / item 1
units.context_stem: ASL-3 model defined by at least one of the following two things:
units.excerpt: Capabilities that significantly increase risk of misuse catastrophe: Access to the model would substantially increase the risk of deliberately-caused catastrophic harm, either by proliferating capabilities, lowering costs, or enabling new methods of attack.
units.paraphrase: One ASL-3 trigger is model access substantially increasing deliberate catastrophic misuse risk via proliferation, lowered cost, or new attack methods.

units.locator: ASL-3 Capabilities and Threat Models / item 1
units.context_stem: Capabilities that significantly increase risk of misuse catastrophe
units.excerpt: This increase in risk is measured relative to today’s baseline level of risk that comes from e.g. access to search engines and textbooks.
units.paraphrase: The increased risk is measured relative to today's baseline risk from sources like search engines and textbooks.

units.locator: ASL-3 Capabilities and Threat Models / item 1
units.context_stem: Capabilities that significantly increase risk of misuse catastrophe
units.excerpt: We expect that AI systems would first elevate this risk from use by non-state attackers7.
units.paraphrase: AI systems are expected to first elevate misuse risk through use by non-state attackers.

units.locator: ASL-3 Capabilities and Threat Models / item 1
units.context_stem: Capabilities that significantly increase risk of misuse catastrophe
units.excerpt: Our first area of effort is in evaluating bioweapons risks where we will determine threat models and capabilities in consultation with a number of world-class biosecurity experts.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic's first evaluation focus is bioweapons risk, with threat models developed alongside leading biosecurity experts.

units.locator: ASL-3 Capabilities and Threat Models / item 1
units.context_stem: Capabilities that significantly increase risk of misuse catastrophe
units.excerpt: We are now developing evaluations for these risks in collaboration with external experts to meet ASL-3 commitments, which will be a more systematized version of our recent work on frontier red-teaming.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic is developing, with external experts, a more systematic version of its frontier red-teaming work to meet ASL-3 commitments.

units.locator: ASL-3 Capabilities and Threat Models / item 1
units.context_stem: Capabilities that significantly increase risk of misuse catastrophe
units.excerpt: In the near future, we anticipate working with CBRN, cyber, and related experts to develop threat models and evaluations in those areas before they present substantial risks.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic anticipates working with CBRN, cyber, and related experts to develop threat models and evaluations proactively before substantial risk arises.

units.locator: ASL-3 Capabilities and Threat Models / item 1
units.context_stem: Capabilities that significantly increase risk of misuse catastrophe
units.excerpt: However, we acknowledge that these evaluations are fundamentally difficult, and there remain disagreements about threat models.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic acknowledges these evaluations are inherently difficult and that threat model disagreements persist.

units.locator: ASL-3 Capabilities and Threat Models / item 2
units.context_stem: ASL-3 model defined by at least one of the following two things:
units.excerpt: Autonomous replication in the lab: The model shows early signs of autonomous self-replication ability, as defined by 50% aggregate success rate on the tasks listed in [Appendix on Autonomy Evaluations].
units.paraphrase: The second ASL-3 trigger is early autonomous self-replication ability, defined as a 50% aggregate success rate on specified appendix tasks.

units.locator: ASL-3 Capabilities and Threat Models / item 2
units.excerpt: The appendix includes an overview of our threat model for autonomous capabilities and a list of the basic capabilities necessary for accumulation of resources and surviving in the real world, along with conditions under which we would judge the model to have succeeded.
units.paraphrase: The appendix describes the autonomy threat model, the basic capabilities needed for resource accumulation and real-world survival, and success conditions.

units.locator: ASL-3 Capabilities and Threat Models / item 2
units.excerpt: Note that the referenced appendix describes the ability to act autonomously specifically in the absence of any human intervention to stop the model, which limits the risk significantly.
units.paraphrase: The appendix's autonomy tests measure ability to act absent human intervention, which limits actual risk significantly.

units.locator: ASL-3 Capabilities and Threat Models / item 2
units.excerpt: Our evaluations were developed in consultation with Paul Christiano and ARC Evals, which specializes in evaluations of autonomous replication.
units.paraphrase: The autonomy evaluations were developed with Paul Christiano and ARC Evals, specialists in autonomous replication evaluation.

units.excerpt: By “non-state attackers” we mean both persistent and opportunistic non-state attackers. This category includes hacker groups, terrorist groups, and industrial espionage but we exclude a small number (~10) of non-state actors with state-level resourcing or backing.
units.paraphrase: "Non-state attackers" includes persistent and opportunistic groups like hackers, terrorists, and industrial spies, excluding roughly ten non-state actors with state-level resources.

units.excerpt: We will consider measures to prevent enhancing the destructive capabilities of these groups and state actors at higher ASLs.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will consider measures against enhancing destructive capabilities of excluded groups and state actors at higher ASLs.

units.locator: ASL-3 Capabilities and Threat Models / para 2
units.excerpt: Note that because safeguards such as Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) or constitutional training can almost certainly be fine-tuned away within the specified 1% of training cost, and also because the ASL-3 standard applies if the model is dangerous at any stage in its training (for example after pretraining but before RLHF), fine-tuning-based safeguards are likely irrelevant to whether a model qualifies as ASL-3.
units.paraphrase: Because RLHF or constitutional training safeguards can likely be removed within the 1% cost threshold, and ASL-3 applies if the model is dangerous at any training stage, fine-tuning-based safeguards are largely irrelevant to ASL-3 qualification.

units.locator: ASL-3 Capabilities and Threat Models / para 2
units.excerpt: To account for the possibility of model theft and subsequent fine-tuning, ASL-3 is intended to characterize the model’s underlying knowledge and abilities, not whether or not its safety features prevent it from cooperating in actually outputting dangerous content (safety features however will be very important in the deployment measures for ASL-3 models).
units.paraphrase: ASL-3 classification reflects the model's underlying knowledge and abilities rather than whether safety features currently block dangerous output, though such features matter for deployment measures.

units.excerpt: A model in the ASL-3 category does not itself present a threat of containment breach due to autonomous self-replication, because it is both unlikely to be able to persist in the real world, and unlikely to overcome even simple security measures intended to prevent it from stealing its own weights.
units.paraphrase: An ASL-3 model does not itself pose containment-breach risk via self-replication, since it is unlikely to survive independently or defeat simple weight-theft security measures.

units.excerpt: However, if the model is stolen and deployed by a malicious or careless actor, there is still (1) a significant risk of catastrophe via weaponized misuse, and (2) a small risk that the model could in fact survive and spread after new developments in post-training improvements, due to the difficulty of estimating how significant such improvements might be in the future.
units.paraphrase: If stolen and misused, an ASL-3 model still poses significant weaponized-misuse risk and a small risk of survival/spread following future post-training improvements.

units.excerpt: Due to the importance of preventing the model weights from being stolen by such a threat actor, the containment measures we commit to implementing prior to training ASL-3 models primarily concern security:
units.paraphrase: Because preventing weight theft is critical, the pre-training ASL-3 containment measures focus primarily on security.

units.context_stem: the containment measures we commit to implementing prior to training ASL-3 models primarily concern security:
units.excerpt: Model weight and code security: We commit to ensuring that ASL-3 models are stored in such a manner to minimize risk of theft by a malicious actor that might use the model to cause a catastrophe.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic commits to storing ASL-3 model weights and code to minimize theft risk by actors who might cause catastrophe.

units.excerpt: Specifically, we will implement measures designed to harden our security so that non-state attackers are unlikely to be able to steal model weights, and advanced threat actors (e.g. states) cannot steal them without significant expense.
units.paraphrase: Security will be hardened so non-state attackers are unlikely to steal weights and state actors face significant cost to do so.

units.excerpt: The full set of security measures that we commit to (and have already started implementing) are described in this appendix, and were developed in consultation with the authors of a forthcoming RAND report on securing AI weights.
units.paraphrase: The full security measures, already begun, are detailed in an appendix and were developed with authors of a forthcoming RAND report on securing AI weights.

units.context_stem: the containment measures we commit to implementing prior to training ASL-3 models primarily concern security:
units.excerpt: Internal compartmentalization: We will limit access to training techniques and model hyperparameters to a need-to-know basis, in order to avoid proliferation of dangerous AI models and the empowerment of bad actors.
units.paraphrase: Access to training techniques and hyperparameters will be limited to need-to-know to prevent proliferation and misuse.

units.excerpt: Some initial practices such as proprietary data classification have already been implemented, though full compartmentalization of code access remains a goal prior to ASL-3.
units.paraphrase: Some compartmentalization practices are already in place, but full code-access compartmentalization is still a goal to be met before ASL-3.

units.context_stem: the containment measures we commit to implementing prior to training ASL-3 models primarily concern security:
units.excerpt: Define and evaluate for ASL-4 warning signs: Before we first train ASL-3 models (i.e. before continuing training beyond when ASL-3 evaluations are triggered), we will develop a definition of ASL-4 capabilities along with warning sign evaluation protocols.
units.paraphrase: Before training ASL-3 models, Anthropic will define ASL-4 capabilities and develop warning sign evaluation protocols.

units.context_stem: Define and evaluate for ASL-4 warning signs
units.excerpt: As with ASL-3, detecting ASL-4 warning signs before corresponding safety/security measures are in place would necessitate pausing training.
units.paraphrase: Detecting ASL-4 warning signs before appropriate safety/security measures exist would require pausing training, as with ASL-3.

units.context_stem: Define and evaluate for ASL-4 warning signs
units.excerpt: We anticipate that an accurate evaluation protocol for ASL-4 may be challenging to develop (for example, a misaligned ASL-4 model could display sufficient awareness to conceal its capabilities under certain testing regimes, and it could also prove hard to predict the capabilities of a large collection of models working together).
units.paraphrase: Anthropic anticipates ASL-4 evaluation protocols will be hard to develop, since a misaligned model might conceal capabilities during testing, and predicting collective model capabilities may be difficult.

units.excerpt: We commit to an additional set of measures for producing ASL-3 model outputs (externally or internally) as compared to merely training or possessing ASL-3 models.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic commits to extra measures for producing ASL-3 model outputs beyond just training or possessing ASL-3 models.

units.excerpt: Successfully pass red-teaming: World-class experts collaborating with prompt engineers should red-team the deployment thoroughly and fail to elicit information at a level of sophistication, accuracy, usefulness, detail, and frequency which significantly enables catastrophic misuse. Misuse domains should at a minimum include causes of extreme CBRN risks, and cybersecurity.
units.paraphrase: World-class experts and prompt engineers must thoroughly red-team deployments and fail to elicit dangerous information, covering at minimum CBRN and cybersecurity misuse.

units.context_stem: Successfully pass red-teaming: World-class experts collaborating with prompt engineers should red-team the deployment thoroughly...
units.excerpt: Note that in contrast to the ASL-3 capability threshold, this red-teaming is about whether the model can cause harm under realistic circumstances (i.e. with harmlessness training and misuse detection in place), not just whether it has the internal knowledge that would enable it in principle to do so.
units.paraphrase: This red-teaming assesses real-world harm potential with safeguards in place, not merely internal capability knowledge.

units.context_stem: Successfully pass red-teaming: World-class experts collaborating with prompt engineers should red-team the deployment thoroughly...
units.excerpt: We will refine this methodology, but we expect it to require at least many dozens of hours of deliberate red-teaming per topic area, by world class experts specifically focused on these threats (rather than students or people with general expertise in a broad domain).
units.paraphrase: Anthropic expects red-teaming to require at least many dozens of hours per topic area by specialized world-class experts.

units.context_stem: Successfully pass red-teaming: World-class experts collaborating with prompt engineers should red-team the deployment thoroughly...
units.excerpt: Additionally, this may involve controlled experiments, where people with similar levels of expertise to real threat actors are divided into groups with and without model access, and we measure the delta of success between them.
units.paraphrase: Red-teaming may include controlled experiments comparing success rates between groups with and without model access.

units.excerpt: Note that ASL-3 deployment measures are cumulative on top of ASL-2 deployment measures; ASL-3 means satisfying both ASL-3 and ASL-2 deployment measures. This is also true for all subsequent levels.
units.paraphrase: ASL-3 deployment measures add to, rather than replace, ASL-2 measures, and this cumulative pattern continues for higher levels.

units.excerpt: Red-team all deployed modalities: If deployment includes e.g. a fine-tuning API, release of weights, or another modality that offers a broader surface area of model modification, red-teaming must include this use of these modalities and must still return a result of no practically important catastrophic misuse.
units.paraphrase: If deployment includes modalities like fine-tuning APIs or weight release, red-teaming must cover those modalities and still show no significant catastrophic misuse potential.

units.context_stem: Red-team all deployed modalities: If deployment includes e.g. a fine-tuning API, release of weights...
units.excerpt: (Note that due to the potential harms presented by ASL-3 models and the possible ease of removing safeguards via fine-tuning, it may be difficult or impossible for these red-teaming tests to pass if weights are released or if unmoderated fine-tuning access is provided).
units.paraphrase: It may be difficult or impossible to pass these red-teaming tests if weights are released or unmoderated fine-tuning is allowed, given ASL-3 model risks.

units.excerpt: Automated detection: As a "defense in depth" addition to harm refusal techniques, classifiers or similar technologies should be deployed to detect and minimize risk of attempts at catastrophic misuse at the user or customer level.
units.paraphrase: Classifiers or similar tools should supplement refusal techniques to detect and minimize catastrophic misuse attempts by users.

units.context_stem: Automated detection: As a "defense in depth" addition to harm refusal techniques...
units.excerpt: We commit to proactively address and mitigate these misuse threats, including working with appropriate law enforcement or national security authorities in the most serious cases.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic commits to proactively addressing misuse threats, including engaging law enforcement or national security authorities for the most serious cases.

units.context_stem: Automated detection: As a "defense in depth" addition to harm refusal techniques...
units.excerpt: ASL-3+ model inputs and outputs should be retained for at least 30 days (by the customer as applicable, e.g. in their cloud account) to assist in the event of an emergency.
units.paraphrase: ASL-3+ model inputs and outputs should be retained for at least 30 days to support emergency response.

units.context_stem: Automated detection: As a "defense in depth" addition to harm refusal techniques...
units.excerpt: We remain committed to data privacy, and will also explore the possibility of exceptions for some low-risk use-cases where safety can be guaranteed.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic remains committed to data privacy and will explore exceptions for low-risk use-cases with guaranteed safety.

units.context_stem: Automated detection: As a "defense in depth" addition to harm refusal techniques...
units.excerpt: This commitment applies only to ASL-3 models, and therefore does not include our current Claude 2 model or represent a change for our current products.
units.paraphrase: This retention commitment applies only to ASL-3 models, excluding Claude 2 or current products.

units.excerpt: Internal usage controls: Automated detection as described above will also apply for internal usage within Anthropic or its distribution partners.
units.paraphrase: The automated detection measures also apply to internal usage by Anthropic and its distribution partners.

units.context_stem: Internal usage controls: Automated detection as described above will also apply for internal usage...
units.excerpt: For internal usage (e.g. red-teaming, RL training, or other R&D activities), generated outputs and corresponding inputs are also logged and retained for at least 30 days for all internal use, including when used for training.
units.paraphrase: Internal usage inputs and outputs, including for red-teaming, RL training or R&D, are logged and retained for at least 30 days.

units.context_stem: Internal usage controls: Automated detection as described above will also apply for internal usage...
units.excerpt: These logs are monitored for abnormal activity, including harmful use or unexpected attempts by AI systems to take real-world actions. Alarms are treated seriously and responded to promptly.
units.paraphrase: Logs are monitored for abnormal activity such as harmful use or AI attempts at real-world actions, with alarms treated seriously and addressed promptly.

units.excerpt: Tiered access: In limited cases, models with capabilities relevant to catastrophic harm may be made available to a select group of vetted users with a legitimate and beneficial use-case that cannot be separated from dangerous capabilities, and only if such access can be granted safely and with sufficient oversight.
units.paraphrase: In limited cases, models with catastrophic-harm-relevant capabilities may be provided to vetted users with legitimate uses that can't be separated from the dangerous capability, if safe and sufficiently overseen.

units.context_stem: Tiered access: In limited cases, models with capabilities relevant to catastrophic harm may be made available...
units.excerpt: For example, potentially harmful biology capabilities that could be used for cancer research might be made available to a small group of vetted researchers at organizations that commit to strong, well defined, and thoroughly vetted security and internal controls.
units.paraphrase: For example, harmful biology capabilities usable for cancer research might be given to vetted researchers at organizations with strong, vetted security controls.

units.excerpt: Vulnerability and incident disclosure: Engage in a vulnerability and incident disclosure process with other labs (subject to security or legal constraints) that covers red-teaming results, national security threats, and autonomous replication threats.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will engage in vulnerability and incident disclosure with other labs, covering red-teaming results and national security/autonomous replication threats, subject to constraints.

units.excerpt: Rapid response to model vulnerabilities: When informed of a newly discovered model vulnerability enabling catastrophic harm (e.g. a jailbreak or a detection failure), we commit to mitigate or patch it promptly (e.g. 50% of the time in which catastrophic harm could realistically occur).
units.paraphrase: Anthropic commits to promptly mitigating or patching newly discovered vulnerabilities enabling catastrophic harm, within roughly 50% of the time such harm could realistically occur.

units.context_stem: Rapid response to model vulnerabilities: When informed of a newly discovered model vulnerability...
units.excerpt: As part of this, Anthropic will maintain a publicly available channel for privately reporting model vulnerabilities.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will maintain a public channel for privately reporting model vulnerabilities.

units.excerpt: The ASLs specify what has to be true substantively of our models and our security to allow safe training and deployment of those models. To ensure this system is implemented in a transparent and trustworthy manner, we additionally make the following procedural commitments.
units.paraphrase: The ASL system defines substantive requirements for safe training and deployment; procedural commitments below ensure transparent, trustworthy implementation.

units.excerpt: These commitments apply at all ASLs but might be modified or strengthened in the future:
units.paraphrase: These procedural commitments apply at every ASL level, though they may be modified or strengthened later.

units.excerpt: Follow an "Update Process" for this document, including approval by the board of directors, following consultation with the Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT). Any updates will be noted and reflected in this document before they are implemented.
units.paraphrase: Updates to the document follow a formal process requiring board approval after consultation with the LTBT, and are recorded before implementation.

units.context_stem: Follow an "Update Process" for this document...
units.excerpt: The most recent version of this document can be found at http://anthropic.com/responsible-scaling-policy.
units.paraphrase: The latest version of the document is available at a specified URL.

units.context_stem: Follow an "Update Process" for this document, including approval by the board of directors...
units.excerpt: We expect most updates to this process to be incremental, for example adding a new ASL level or slightly modifying the set of evaluations or security procedures as we learn more about model safety features or unexpected capabilities.
units.paraphrase: Most updates are expected to be incremental, such as adding an ASL level or modifying evaluations/procedures as understanding grows.

units.context_stem: Follow an "Update Process" for this document, including approval by the board of directors...
units.excerpt: However, in a situation of extreme emergency, such as when a clearly bad actor (such as a rogue state) is scaling in so reckless a manner that it is likely to lead to lead to imminent global catastrophe if not stopped (and where AI itself is helpful in such defense), we could envisage a substantial loosening of these restrictions as an emergency response.
units.paraphrase: In an extreme emergency, such as reckless scaling by a bad actor threatening imminent global catastrophe, Anthropic could envisage substantially loosening these restrictions.

units.context_stem: Follow an "Update Process" for this document, including approval by the board of directors...
units.excerpt: Such action would only be taken in consultation with governmental authorities, and the compelling case for it would be presented publicly to the extent possible.
units.paraphrase: Any emergency loosening would only occur in consultation with government authorities, with the rationale made public where possible.

units.excerpt: Distribution partner safety evaluation: Our distribution partners contribute substantially to the reach and adoption of our models. Anthropic must therefore ensure that they abide by our safety protocols when using or licensing Anthropic AI systems.
units.paraphrase: Because distribution partners drive substantial reach and adoption, Anthropic must ensure they follow its safety protocols.

units.context_stem: Distribution partner safety evaluation: Our distribution partners contribute substantially...
units.excerpt: This ensures responsible scaling through our entire ecosystem and for all applications of our technology.
units.paraphrase: This ensures responsible scaling extends throughout the ecosystem and all applications of the technology.

units.context_stem: Distribution partner safety evaluation: Our distribution partners contribute substantially...
units.excerpt: Distribution partnership contracts will be verified for compatibility with the ASL system and must have a mechanism to bind the partner's use of Anthropic models to the same or similar safety measures as Anthropic (e.g. similar security measures) in order to address catastrophic risks.
units.paraphrase: Distribution partnership contracts must be checked for ASL compatibility and include mechanisms binding partners to comparable safety measures.

units.excerpt: Document and test internal safety procedures. This includes pausing training in response to evaluation warning signs, restricting internal model access, safety review of new training runs and deployments, and responding to vulnerabilities in deployed models (including, for ASL-3+ models, the ability to restrict access in the case of an extreme safety emergency that cannot otherwise be mitigated).
units.paraphrase: Internal safety procedures must be documented and tested, covering pausing training on warning signs, restricting access, safety review, and vulnerability response, including emergency access restriction for ASL-3+ models.

units.excerpt: Proactively plan for a pause in scaling. We will manage our plans and finances to support a pause in model training if one proves necessary, or an extended delay between training and deployment of more advanced models if that proves necessary.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will manage plans and finances to be able to pause training or delay deployment of advanced models if needed.

units.context_stem: Proactively plan for a pause in scaling. We will manage our plans and finances...
units.excerpt: During such a pause, we would work to implement security or other measures required to support safe training and deployment, while also ensuring our partners have continued access to their present tier of models (which will have previously passed safety evaluations).
units.paraphrase: During a pause, Anthropic would implement needed safety measures while ensuring partners keep access to their current, already-evaluated model tier.

units.excerpt: Publicly share evaluation results after model deployment where possible, in some cases in the initial model card, in other cases with a delay if it serves a broad safety interest.
units.paraphrase: Evaluation results will be publicly shared after deployment where possible, sometimes in the model card and sometimes delayed for broad safety reasons.

units.excerpt: Share results of ASL evaluations promptly with Anthropic's governing bodies, including the board of directors and LTBT, in order to sufficiently inform them of changes to our risk profile.
units.paraphrase: ASL evaluation results will be shared promptly with the board and LTBT to keep them informed of risk profile changes.

units.excerpt: Responsible Scaling Officer. There is a designated member of staff responsible for ensuring that our Responsible Scaling Commitments are executed properly.
units.paraphrase: A designated staff member, the Responsible Scaling Officer, is responsible for ensuring proper execution of the commitments.

units.context_stem: Responsible Scaling Officer. There is a designated member of staff...
units.excerpt: Each quarter, they will share a report on implementation status to our board and LTBT, explicitly noting any deficiencies in implementation.
units.paraphrase: Quarterly, the officer will report implementation status, explicitly noting deficiencies, to the board and LTBT.

units.context_stem: Responsible Scaling Officer. There is a designated member of staff...
units.excerpt: They will also be responsible for sharing ad hoc updates sooner if there are any substantial implementation failures.
units.paraphrase: The officer will also share ad hoc updates promptly if substantial implementation failures occur.

units.excerpt: Implement a non-compliance reporting policy for our Responsible Scaling Commitments as part of reaching ASL-3. The policy should allow for anonymous feedback, with an appropriate reporting chain.
units.paraphrase: A non-compliance reporting policy allowing anonymous feedback with an appropriate reporting chain must be implemented upon reaching ASL-3.

units.excerpt: Ensuring that we never train a model that passes an ASL evaluation threshold is a difficult task. Models are trained in discrete sizes, they require effort to evaluate mid-training, and serious, meaningful evaluations may be very time consuming, since they will likely require fine-tuning.
units.paraphrase: Preventing training a model past an ASL threshold is difficult due to discrete training sizes and the time-consuming nature of meaningful evaluations requiring fine-tuning.

units.excerpt: This means there is a risk of overshooting an ASL threshold when we intended to stop short of it.
units.paraphrase: There is thus a risk of overshooting the intended ASL threshold.

units.excerpt: We mitigate this risk by creating a buffer: we have intentionally designed our ASL evaluations to trigger at slightly lower capability levels than those we are concerned about, while ensuring we evaluate at defined, regular intervals (specifically every 4x increase in effective compute, as defined below) in order to limit the amount of overshoot that is possible.
units.paraphrase: This overshoot risk is mitigated by a buffer: evaluations trigger below actual concern levels and occur at regular intervals of every 4x increase in effective compute.

units.excerpt: We have aimed to set the size of our safety buffer to 6x (larger than our 4x evaluation interval) so model training can continue safely while evaluations take place.
units.paraphrase: The safety buffer is aimed at 6x, larger than the 4x evaluation interval, to allow safe continued training during evaluation.

units.excerpt: Correct execution of this scheme will result in us training models that just barely pass the test for ASL-N, are still slightly below our actual threshold of concern (due to our buffer), and then pausing training and deployment of that model unless the corresponding safety measures are ready.
units.paraphrase: If executed correctly, models will just barely pass the ASL-N test while remaining below the true concern threshold, with training and deployment paused unless safety measures are ready.

units.excerpt: Model evaluations: Evaluations are tests that are designed to detect dangerous capabilities. They should be conservative "warning signs" so as to avoid accidentally overshooting a critical safety threshold.
units.paraphrase: Evaluations are tests to detect dangerous capabilities and should be conservative warning signs to avoid overshooting critical thresholds.

units.context_stem: Model evaluations: Evaluations are tests that are designed to detect dangerous capabilities...
units.excerpt: Progressive difficulty: Evaluations may also consist of multiple difficulty stages, such that later stages are only run if earlier evaluations show warning signs (e.g. we might run a simple multiple choice eval for certain risks, avoiding a more thorough evaluation unless the model achieves high performance on this simpler eval).
units.paraphrase: Evaluations may have progressive difficulty stages, running more thorough tests only after earlier simpler evaluations show warning signs.

units.context_stem: Model evaluations: Evaluations are tests that are designed to detect dangerous capabilities...
units.excerpt: Previous evaluations: We previously carried out similar evaluations on a model similar to Claude 2 for capabilities related to biological risks and collaborated with the Alignment Research Center to evaluate autonomous capabilities. Both evaluations showed the model as strictly below ASL-3.
units.paraphrase: Similar prior evaluations of a Claude 2-like model for biological risk and autonomous capability (with ARC) showed results strictly below ASL-3.

units.excerpt: Timing: During model training and fine-tuning, Anthropic will conduct an evaluation of its models for next-ASL capabilities both (1) after every 4x jump in effective compute, including if this occurs mid-training, and (2) every 3 months to monitor fine-tuning/tooling/etc improvements.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic will evaluate models for next-ASL capabilities after every 4x jump in effective compute and every 3 months to monitor fine-tuning improvements.

units.context_stem: Timing: During model training and fine-tuning, Anthropic will conduct an evaluation...
units.excerpt: Effective Compute: We define effective compute as roughly the amount of compute it would have taken to train a model if no improvements to pretraining or fine-tuning techniques are included. This is operationalized by tracking the scaling of model capabilities (e.g. cross-entropy loss on a test set).
units.paraphrase: Effective compute is defined as the compute needed absent pretraining/fine-tuning improvements, operationalized via tracking model capability scaling such as cross-entropy loss.

units.excerpt: Investment in evaluations: An inherent difficulty of an evaluations regime is that it is not currently possible to truly upper-bound the capabilities of generative models.
units.paraphrase: A core challenge of the evaluations regime is the impossibility of truly upper-bounding generative model capabilities.

units.context_stem: Investment in evaluations: An inherent difficulty of an evaluations regime...
units.excerpt: However, it is important that we are evaluating models with close to our best capabilities elicitation techniques, to avoid underestimating the capabilities it would be possible for a malicious actor to elicit if the model were stolen.
units.paraphrase: Evaluations must use near-best elicitation techniques to avoid underestimating what a malicious actor could elicit from a stolen model.

units.context_stem: Investment in evaluations: An inherent difficulty of an evaluations regime...
units.excerpt: False negatives due to harmlessness: While there are commercial and research incentives to develop maximally effective post-training techniques, certain evaluations may result in false negatives when used on commercial models.
units.paraphrase: Despite incentives for effective post-training, evaluations run on commercial models may produce false negatives.

units.context_stem: Investment in evaluations: An inherent difficulty of an evaluations regime...
units.excerpt: For example, harmlessness techniques may cause the model to refuse to assist with dangerous activities even when the underlying capability is present. Proper effort must be invested to avoid this type of false negative.
units.paraphrase: Harmlessness training may cause refusals masking present dangerous capability, so effort must be invested to avoid such false negatives.

units.context_stem: Investment in evaluations: An inherent difficulty of an evaluations regime...
units.excerpt: Mid-training evaluations: For significant scale-ups, it may be necessary to perform evaluations mid-training. Such models may have capability limitations due to various (potentially slow or expensive) fine-tuning stages having not yet occurred, or because performance may not scale linearly with compute in the midst of training.
units.paraphrase: Significant scale-ups may require mid-training evaluations, though such models may have limitations from incomplete fine-tuning or nonlinear scaling.

units.context_stem: Investment in evaluations: An inherent difficulty of an evaluations regime...
units.excerpt: For now, we commit to perform mid-training fine-tuning and evaluations which, combined with the safety buffer described above, are intended to mitigate the risk of passing the defined ASL-3 threshold mid-training.
units.paraphrase: Anthropic commits to mid-training fine-tuning and evaluations, which with the safety buffer aim to mitigate the risk of exceeding ASL-3 mid-training.

units.context_stem: Investment in evaluations: An inherent difficulty of an evaluations regime...
units.excerpt: We expect to update our procedures in the future as we better understand how to perform mid-training evaluations, for example by adjusting task difficulty to account for the limitations of a mid-training model.
units.paraphrase: Procedures are expected to be updated as understanding of mid-training evaluations improves, such as adjusting task difficulty for mid-training limitations.

units.context_stem: Investment in evaluations: An inherent difficulty of an evaluations regime...
units.excerpt: At high safety levels, we may transition to doing full fine-tuning even for mid-training evals in order to further mitigate risks of underestimating capabilities.
units.paraphrase: At higher safety levels, full fine-tuning may be used even for mid-training evaluations to further reduce underestimation risk.

units.excerpt: Response policy: If an evaluation threshold triggers, we will follow the following procedure:
units.paraphrase: If an evaluation threshold is triggered, a defined response procedure will be followed.

units.context_stem: Response policy: If an evaluation threshold triggers, we will follow the following procedure:
units.excerpt: (1) If sufficient Containment Measures for the next ASL have already been implemented, ensure they are activated before continuing training.
units.paraphrase: If sufficient containment measures for the next ASL are already implemented, they must be activated before continuing training.

units.context_stem: Response policy: If an evaluation threshold triggers, we will follow the following procedure:
units.excerpt: (2) If sufficient measures are not yet implemented, pause training and analyze the level of risk presented by the model. In particular, conduct a thorough analysis to determine whether the evaluation was overly conservative, or whether the model indeed presents near-next-ASL risks.
units.paraphrase: If measures aren't ready, training is paused and the model's risk level is thoroughly analyzed to determine if the evaluation was overly conservative or the model genuinely poses near-next-ASL risk.

units.context_stem: Response policy: If an evaluation threshold triggers, we will follow the following procedure:
units.excerpt: (2a) If the evaluation is determined to be overly conservative (i.e. creating a greater than 6x "safety buffer") and the model is confirmed to not pose (or be close to posing) next-ASL risks, construct new evaluations that take into account this new information.
units.paraphrase: If the evaluation is found overly conservative (more than a 6x safety buffer) and the model doesn't pose near-next-ASL risk, new evaluations incorporating this information will be constructed.

units.context_stem: Response policy: If an evaluation threshold triggers, we will follow the following procedure:
units.excerpt: This document will be updated according to the "Update Process" described above before continuing training.
units.paraphrase: The document will be updated via the Update Process before training continues in this scenario.

units.context_stem: Response policy: If an evaluation threshold triggers, we will follow the following procedure:
units.excerpt: (2b) If the model is determined to be close to next-ASL risk, do not resume training until the next safety level has been defined (with this document updated accordingly) and its Containment Measures have been implemented.
units.paraphrase: If the model is close to next-ASL risk, training will not resume until the next safety level is defined and its containment measures implemented.

units.context_stem: Response policy: If an evaluation threshold triggers, we will follow the following procedure:
units.excerpt: (2c) If the model has already surpassed the next ASL during training, immediately lock down access to the weights. Stakeholders including the CISO and CEO should be immediately convened to determine whether the level of danger merits deletion of the weights.
units.paraphrase: If the model has already surpassed the next ASL during training, weight access is immediately locked down and the CISO, CEO, and other stakeholders convene to decide on possible weight deletion.

units.context_stem: Response policy: If an evaluation threshold triggers, we will follow the following procedure:
units.excerpt: After a detailed post-mortem, this policy should then be promptly updated to minimize risk of the re-occurrence of this failure (e.g. through more frequent or thorough evaluations).
units.paraphrase: Following a detailed post-mortem, the policy should be promptly updated to reduce recurrence risk, e.g. via more frequent or thorough evaluations.

units.context_stem: Response policy: If an evaluation threshold triggers, we will follow the following procedure:
